sentences.text: Anurognathus possessed a short head equipped with pin-like teeth adapted for catching insects.
Studies revealed that the skull was very short and broad, being wider than it was long.
The animal had an estimated wingspan of fifty centimeters and a body length of nine centimeters including the skull.
Evidence of a membrane near the shin indicated that the wing contacted the ankle, resulting in a short and broad wing shape.

This creature was featured in the second episode of the BBC documentary Walking with Dinosaurs, appearing in a mutual symbiotic relationship with the dinosaur Diplodocus, eating parasites from its skin.
It also appeared in the fifth episode of the ITV sci-fi series Primeval, where it was incorrectly depicted living in the Late Cretaceous, 85 million years ago, with piranha-like behavior.
A flock was shown devouring the flesh of a carcass in minutes, a strange behavior considering anatomical evidence shows this species was an insectivore more similar to modern podargos.
Ludwig Döderlein first named and described the genus in 1923.
The genus is based on the holotype BSP 1922.I.42, found in the Solnhofen Limestone near Eichstätt.
The holotype was redescribed by Peter Wellnhofer in 1975.
A second, smaller specimen, likely a subadult, was found later; its plates were sold to private collections without official records and were described by S. Christopher Bennet in 2007.
Anurognathus likely possessed very large eyes supported by enormous orbits, providing high visual acuity in dim light and some binocular vision due to forward-pointing eyes.
S. Christopher Bennett inferred that the animal was a slower-flying predator specialized in maneuverability, with large eyes adapted for a crepuscular lifestyle.
Research predicting a gape of 1734 mm² for the species concluded that its prey would have been very small, around 11 mm in length.
Researcher S. Christopher Bennett interpreted bumps on the holotype jaws as evidence of a protruding bristle formed by hairs on the snout.
Oskar Kuhn assigned Anurognathus to the family Anurognathidae in 1937.
A 2021 phylogenetic analysis by Xuefang Wei and colleagues placed Anurognathus within the subfamily Anurognathinae of the family Anurognathidae.
In the current clade Anurognathidae, Anurognathus is the sister taxon to the clade Asiaticognathidae, which contains the genera Batrachognathus, Dendrorhynchoides, and Jeholopterus.
The type species of the genus is Anurognathus ammoni.
Anurognathus lived approximately 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic (Tithonian) in Europe, specifically in the Altmühltal Formation of Germany.
The species lived during the Tithonian stage, from 149.2 to 145.06 million years ago.
Ludwig Döderlein originally suggested that Anurognathus was a swift flyer similar to a modern nightjar, a view later challenged by findings of shorter wings.
According to Döderlein, the animal was a fast flyer that surprised its prey with its long wings, similar to the modern swift.

However, Bennet inferred from the discovery of the true short wing size combined with the short tail that it was a slow-flying predator specialized in hunting with maneuverability, with large eyes adapted to a crepuscular lifestyle.
